name: Vulkan
summary: An explicit graphics and compute API that separates device resources, command recording, queue submission, and synchronization so applications control much of execution and lifetime ordering.

features.name: Explicit device and resource lifecycle
features.description: Vulkan applications create and destroy instances, physical/logical devices, memory, images, buffers, descriptor objects, and pipelines through explicit handles and allocation decisions.
benefits: Exposes resource and capability decisions needed for predictable performance
costs: Applications carry substantial lifetime, compatibility, and allocation bookkeeping

features.name: Record and submit command separation
features.description: Vulkan records commands into command buffers and submits them to queues; recording and submission are distinct from execution, permitting application-controlled batching and multi-queue scheduling.
benefits: Supports batching and explicit scheduling across queues
costs: Command-buffer reuse and queue ownership require careful synchronization

features.name: Explicit synchronization contract
features.description: Vulkan requires applications to describe relevant ordering and visibility through synchronization primitives and pipeline barriers, including resource layout and access transitions.
benefits: Makes dependency and visibility costs explicit to implementations and tools
costs: Incorrect barriers cause races, validation failures, or unnecessary stalls

mathematical_views.model: Dependency DAG of commands and resources
mathematical_views.question: Which execution and memory dependencies must hold between recorded commands, resources, and queue submissions?
assumptions: Commands and resource accesses are graph vertices and labeled edges
Edges represent required ordering or visibility, not a complete driver schedule
The graph is acyclic for the modeled submission segment

mathematical_views.question: Which resource and command-buffer transitions are valid from creation through use and destruction?
assumptions: Handle lifecycle states are modeled explicitly
Host/device concurrency is represented only where the specification defines a synchronization requirement

benefits: Fine-grained control of capabilities, memory, and ownership
costs: More application code and more invalid states to prevent

benefits: Batchable work submission and queue-level scheduling
costs: Recorded work can become stale or expensive to coordinate

benefits: Predictable dependency visibility and lower hidden driver work
costs: Barrier correctness and tuning are difficult
